name: Sara Rossi

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time, Sara. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. Everything you say stays confidential, so feel free to tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. To start, could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I work at a mid-size supermarket in a market town, the one opposite the Thursday market. I do the tills in the mornings and help in the in-store bakery in the afternoons, shaping rolls and filling the bread shelves. I love the bakery, the smell gets into my coat and my husband says I come home smelling like toast. What wears me out is the till on market day, when the whole town comes in at once.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: How long have you been there, and what's home like?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Eight years, and I'm on the better rate because I cover two departments. I'm married to Luca, who's a joiner, and we bought a little terraced house last year. We've still got about eight months of pay saved after the deposit. I use AI now and then, for recipes or writing the parish newsletter, but I don't rely on it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say good, people worry too much about new things. At work I'd say it's back to normal. I might mention it after church, if anyone asked.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: For me, nothing changes. The bakery is hands-on and the tills are steady. My worries are the mortgage rate and when we start a family.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep both jobs at the store and keep paying the mortgage. We'd think about a baby in a year or two. I might ask about becoming a proper baker in the store.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, mostly content.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The mortgage rate worries you. How much?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Our fixed rate ends in three years, and if it goes up, that's maybe a hundred and fifty more a month. We can manage it with savings. It's on my mind though.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why the bakery over the tills?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because I make something. You put dough in and bread comes out, and people buy it warm. The till is just beeping.

say: I'd say people **worry too much** about new things.
I'd tell colleagues it's **back to normal**, and mention it after church if asked.
think: Nothing changes, because the **bakery** is hands-on and the tills are steady.
My worries are the **mortgage rate** and when we start a family.
do: Keep both jobs at the store and keep paying the **mortgage**.
Ask about becoming a **proper baker** and plan a baby in a year or two.
S0.quote: You put dough in and bread comes out, and people buy it warm.
fieldNote: She takes real **pride** in bakery work over the till.
Her quiet pressure is the **fixed mortgage** rate ending in three years.
Plans for a **family** sit at the centre of her life.

steps.text: Keep the morning tills and afternoon bakery shifts
Plan to start a family with Luca in a year or two
Ask the store about training as a proper baker

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's change, and you get on with it. At work I'd say people should learn what's useful and not moan. At church I'd say look after each other.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think the tills will shrink slowly as robots come in. The thinking stuff, like ordering and rotas, is head office's job. I think people like a person making their bread, so the bakery is safer than the till.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask to move fully into the bakery and give up the till shifts. I'd look at a baking apprenticeship once I see a colleague try one. We'd save a bit more before the baby, maybe a hundred extra a month.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A little uneasy, but steady.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you use more AI in this world?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A bit, if the store gives us a tool for bakery orders. I'd try it after someone else shows me. I'm not one to go first.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell Luca?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That we keep calm and keep saving. His joinery is safe for now, people always need doors and stairs. We'd just push the baby back a little.

say: I'd say it's **change**, and you get on with it.
I'd tell colleagues to **learn what's useful** and not moan.
think: The **tills** will shrink slowly as robots arrive.
The **bakery** feels safer, because people like a person making their bread.
do: Move fully into the **bakery** and give up till shifts.
Try a **baking apprenticeship** once a colleague does, saving £100 more monthly.
S1.quote: I think people like a person making their bread, so the bakery is safer than the till.
fieldNote: She moves toward the **craft** part of her job.
She'll try new tools **after others** show the way.
The **baby** gets pushed back a little, not cancelled.

steps.text: Ask to move fully into the in-store bakery
Save 100 extra a month before having a baby
Push back plans for a baby by about a year

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we need to look after families and keep apprenticeships going, not just hand out cheques. I'd say it after church and to friends. I wouldn't post much.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I think the tills go by 2031, and the bakery too, once robots can shape dough. The 2028 bit hits the ordering, which isn't mine. But in five years my whole job is likely gone.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd start a proper baking apprenticeship straight away, at a small independent bakery in town. We'd put off the baby for a couple of years. I'd keep the savings for the mortgage if Luca's work dips.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. It'd sit heavy on me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why an independent bakery, if robots can bake?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because a small baker sells the person as much as the bread. People come in for the chat and the sourdough they know. A big factory will get robots first.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What gets cut at home?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Holidays first, then eating out. We'd keep the house, that's the priority. Luca's mum would help if things got bad.

say: I'd say we must look after **families** and keep apprenticeships, not hand out cheques.
I'd say it **after church** and to friends, not much online.
think: The tills go by **2031**, and the bakery once robots can shape dough.
In **five years** my whole job is likely gone.
do: Start a **baking apprenticeship** at an independent bakery straight away.
Put off the **baby** two years and keep savings for the mortgage.
feel: **Anxious**, with it sitting heavy on her.
S2.quote: A small baker sells the person as much as the bread.
fieldNote: She bets on **small independents** keeping people longer than factories.
The **baby** is the first plan she delays.
Her **traditional values** show in wanting apprenticeships over cheques.

steps.text: Start a baking apprenticeship at an independent town bakery
Put off having a baby for about two years
Cut holidays and eating out to protect the mortgage
Lean on Luca's mum if money gets tight

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is enough to plan, so families should start now. I'd say the government should back apprenticeships. I'd stay calm about it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd have until about 2034 on the shop floor. That's time to do an apprenticeship and maybe have a baby. It's tight but doable.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd start the baking apprenticeship next year. We'd try for a baby once I've finished it. I'd keep saving about two hundred a month.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Worried, but it feels manageable.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is it a bit much, a new trade and a baby at once?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe. But women have always done more than one thing at a time. My mum ran a café with three of us at home.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who at work would you worry about?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Our till supervisor Gwen, who's near sixty. She'd struggle to start over. I'd hope the company helps her retire early.

I'd say the government should **back apprenticeships**.

do: Try for a **baby** after finishing it and save £200 a month.
S3.quote: My mum ran a café with three of us at home.
fieldNote: Five years lets her fit an **apprenticeship** before a baby.
Her **mother's café** is her model for juggling work and family.

steps.text: Start a baking apprenticeship next year

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is plenty, so no excuses for anyone. I'd say families should plan like they'd plan for a baby. Sensible, not scared.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd be thirty-seven when robots arrive. By then I'd want to be a qualified baker, maybe running a small place. The tills carry me until then.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: We'd have a baby in the next two years as we planned. I'd do the baking apprenticeship after maternity leave. I'd keep saving and paying the mortgage.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A bit uneasy at the back of my mind, but mostly settled.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you want your own bakery one day?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe with Luca, he could build the counters. A small family place on the high street. That'd be a dream.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Anything about this world still bother you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That young people won't learn trades because they think there's time. My nephew wants to be an influencer. I'd tell my nephew to learn to bake bread or fix pipes, not to chase likes.

say: I'd say **ten years** is plenty, so no excuses.
I'd tell families to plan for it like **planning for a baby**.
think: I'd be **thirty-seven** when robots arrive, ideally a qualified baker running a small place.
The **tills** carry me until then, which is a long while.
do: Have a **baby** in the next two years as planned.
Do the **baking apprenticeship** after maternity leave and keep saving.
feel: A bit **uneasy** at the back of her mind, mostly settled.
S4.quote: I'd tell my nephew to learn to bake bread or fix pipes, not to chase likes.
fieldNote: A decade lets her keep the **baby plan** on schedule.
She dreams of a **family bakery** with her joiner husband.
Her worry shifts to young people **skipping trades**.

steps.text: Have a baby with Luca in the next two years
Do a baking apprenticeship after maternity leave
Keep saving while paying the mortgage

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028, because it'd land just as we'd want a baby. What would help is paid apprenticeships for adults and help for small family bakeries. Not handouts, a chance to work.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe ask about faith. Our church would rally round if people lost jobs, and that counts for a lot.

headlineQuote: Our church would rally round if people lost jobs, and that counts for a lot.
portrait: Sara is a **27-year-old** cashier and bakery helper in a market-town supermarket, eight years in.
She's married to Luca, a joiner, with a new **mortgage** and eight months saved.
She loves the **bakery** and sees baking as her safer, hands-on future.
Faster AGI makes her **delay a baby** and start an apprenticeship sooner.
She favours **apprenticeships** and family support over handouts.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, because it would land just as they'd want a baby.
whatWouldHelp: **Paid apprenticeships** for adults and help for small family bakeries, not handouts.
